say: You give it the unit circle and an angle $A$. It builds the formula $\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1$ from **Pythagoras**.
The point at angle $A$ has coordinates $(\cos A, \sin A)$, and it sits exactly 1 from the centre. Pythagoras on that distance is the whole proof.

example.question: The point $P$ lies on the unit circle, at angle $A$ from the positive $x$-axis. Use the right-angled triangle formed by $P$ to prove that $\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1$.

steps.title: Draw the triangle
steps.say: Draw the unit circle, with centre $O$ and radius $1$. Put $P$ at angle $A$ and drop a vertical line from $P$ to the $x$-axis. That makes a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse $OP = 1$.

lines.text: Hypotenuse $|OP| = 1$, because $P$ is on the unit circle.

steps.title: Read off the sides
steps.say: By definition, the coordinates of $P$ are $(\cos A, \sin A)$. So the horizontal side is $\hl{1}{\cos A}$ and the vertical side is $\hl{2}{\sin A}$.

steps.title: Apply Pythagoras
steps.say: In a right-angled triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides add to the square of the hypotenuse. Write that with the sides from the last step.

steps.title: Any angle
steps.say: For an angle in another quadrant a coordinate is negative, but squaring removes the sign. The result holds for every $A$.

say: You give it a sum or difference of two angles, $A \pm B$. It writes the sine, cosine or tangent of it in terms of $\sin$ and $\cos$ of $A$ and $B$ **separately**.
To find an exact value, split the angle into two you already know, such as $30°$, $45°$, $60°$ or $90°$, then put their exact values into the formula.

how.higher: On Paper 2 it is usually a 10 mark part: find an exact value such as $\sin 75°$, or prove $\tan(A \pm B)$ in 2015 and 2022. It also sits inside bigger proofs, such as the De Moivre induction in 2018.

example.question: Use a compound angle formula to find the exact value of $\cos 105°$. Give your answer in surd form.

steps.title: Split the angle
steps.say: We know exact values for $\hl{1}{60°}$ and $\hl{2}{45°}$, and they add to $105°$. So write $105°$ as $\hl{1}{60°} + \hl{2}{45°}$.

steps.title: Write the formula
steps.say: Cosine of a sum is cosine times cosine **minus** sine times sine. Write the formula, with $A = \hl{1}{60°}$ and $B = \hl{2}{45°}$.

steps.title: Rationalise
steps.say: Multiply the top and bottom by $\sqrt{2}$ to remove the surd from the bottom.

higher.tip: Split the angle into two you know exactly, such as $30° + 45°$. Writing the split earns work-of-merit credit before any formula is used.
Substitute the two exact values into the formula in full. That line alone reaches high partial credit.

say: You give it an equation such as $\sin 2x = k$. It finds **every** solution in the range you are given.
Solve for the whole angle $2x$ first, over the longer range it covers, and divide by $2$ only at the end.

how.higher: On Paper 2 it is a part of its own, 5 to 15 marks, in most years from 2015 to 2024. Some are in degrees and some in radians, and some ask for the general solution with $n$.

example.question: Solve $\sin 2x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$. Give your answers in radians, in terms of $\pi$.

steps.title: Find the reference angle
steps.say: Ignore the minus sign and find the acute angle with $\sin = \frac{1}{2}$. This is the **reference angle**.

steps.title: Choose the quadrants
steps.say: Sine is negative in the 3rd and 4th quadrants. Measure $2x$ from the reference angle $\hl{1}{\frac{\pi}{6}}$ in each one.

steps.title: Add full turns
steps.say: Since $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, the angle $2x$ runs from $0$ to $4\pi$. Add $2\pi$ to each answer to find the second lap.

lines.text: Adding $2\pi$ again would pass $4\pi$, so stop.

steps.title: Divide by 2
steps.say: Now divide each of the four values of $2x$ by $2$ to get $x$.

higher.tip: Name the quadrants and the reference angle. Both earn partial credit before any value of the angle is found.
Write each value of the multiple angle, such as $2x$, as well as the final $x$. Values of $2x$ found without the divide-by-2 step still earn high partial credit.
For a radian question, set the calculator to radians. Degree mode costs a mark even if the rest is right.
Write the general solution with $n$, then put in $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$ until you leave the range, so no solution is missed.

say: You give it the numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ in $a + b\cos c\theta$, or the graph itself. It finds the **period** and the **range**, or goes the other way.
The period is $\frac{2\pi}{c}$. The graph swings $|b|$ above and below the middle line $a$, so the range is $[a - |b|,\ a + |b|]$.

how.higher: On both papers it is the most examined trigonometry skill, in every year but 2019, 2020 and 2025. Usually it is a short 5 mark part asking for the period and range of a model such as tides, volume of air or current, and sometimes a sketch.

example.question: The depth of water in a harbour is modelled by $h(t) = 8 + 3\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\right)$ metres, where $t$ is the time in hours. Find the period and the range of $h$.

steps.title: Match the form
steps.say: Compare with $a + b\cos ct$. Here $a = 8$, $b = 3$ and $c = \frac{\pi}{6}$.

steps.title: Find the period
steps.say: One full wave takes $\frac{2\pi}{c}$ hours. Put in $c = \frac{\pi}{6}$.

steps.title: Find the range
steps.say: The cosine swings between $-1$ and $1$, so $h$ swings $3$ above and $3$ below the middle value $8$. Work out the lowest and highest depth.

steps.title: State the range
steps.say: Write the range as an interval from the lowest value $\hl{2}{5}$ to the highest $\hl{3}{11}$.

higher.tip: Say which value is the maximum and which is the minimum. Giving $2$ and $40$ without labels loses a mark.
Keep the period and the range apart. Swapping them loses a mark.
When you sketch, show a sine curve of at least one full period and mark both the period and the range on the axes.

sources.quote: sine curve of at least one period,

higher.tip: Check the calculator mode. Degrees when the question is in radians costs a mark.
